meta.name: Microsoft Azure Solutions Architect Expert (AZ-305)
meta.notes: [hardening pass: distractor rebalance on 32 questions — removed length tells (".", ",.", ";."), padded short-correct options to within ~10% of distractors, trimmed long-correct options where dominant]

questions.question: A large enterprise needs to enforce that all Azure resources must be deployed only in specific regions (West Europe and North Europe) across 80 subscriptions. New subscriptions added in the future must automatically comply. What is the MOST scalable approach?
options: Create a custom RBAC role in each subscription that restricts deployment to those regions
Use Azure Blueprints to deploy resource locks in each subscription denying deployments outside the target regions
Enable Azure Defender and configure geo-restriction alerts for deployments in non-approved regions
Configure Azure Policy 'Allowed locations' initiative at the Management Group level and assign it to the root management
questions.explanation: Azure Policy assigned at a Management Group scope applies to ALL subscriptions within that group hierarchy, including subscriptions added in the future. The built-in 'Allowed locations' policy definition (or an initiative containing it) enforces the region constraint at creation time with a Deny effect. RBAC cannot restrict deployment regions. Blueprints are a deployment mechanism, not a continuous enforcement control. Azure Defender is a threat detection service. it automatically applies to all current and future subscriptions underneath

questions.question: A solutions architect must design an identity solution for a company with 10,000 on-premises Active Directory users who need SSO access to Azure resources and Microsoft 365. The company cannot allow password hashes to be stored in the cloud for compliance reasons. Which hybrid identity method satisfies this requirement?
options: Password Hash Synchronization (PHS) — synchronize password hashes from on-premises AD to Azure AD for cloud authentication
Pass-Through Authentication (PTA) — install lightweight agents on-premises that validate passwords against AD without storing hashes in the cloud
ADFS federation via Azure AD Connect — authentication happens on-premises through ADFS servers; Azure AD acts only as a relying party
Azure AD B2C with custom policies and a SAML federation back to the on-premises directory for hybrid identity
questions.explanation: Pass-Through Authentication (PTA) validates users' passwords directly against on-premises Active Directory. No password hashes or tokens are stored in Azure AD — the authentication agent on-premises handles validation and returns a success/fail response. This satisfies compliance requirements that prohibit cloud storage of password hashes. ADFS federation also works but requires significant on-premises infrastructure. PHS explicitly stores password hashes in Azure AD, violating the requirement.

questions.question: An architect needs to grant a team of junior developers access to create and manage resources within a specific resource group, but prevent them from modifying any IAM/RBAC assignments. Which RBAC role combination achieves least-privilege?
options: Assign the Owner role at the resource group scope to give the team full resource management capability
Assign the Reader role plus a custom role with write permissions on specific resource provider types
Assign the Contributor role at the resource group scope so the team can create and manage resources without IAM rights
Assign the User Access Administrator role scoped to the resource group for full access control management
questions.explanation: The built-in Contributor role provides full rights to create, delete, and manage resources but explicitly does NOT include Microsoft.Authorization/* actions (assigning/removing roles, creating policy assignments). This is the correct least-privilege choice: full resource management without IAM modification rights. Owner includes Microsoft.Authorization/* which allows granting access. User Access Administrator is specifically for managing role assignments, the opposite of what's needed.

questions.question: A company's operations team needs to collect OS-level performance metrics (custom memory counters, application logs) from 500 Azure VMs and on-premises servers into a central workspace for dashboards and alerts. Which Azure Monitor component collects this data?
options: Azure Monitor Agent (AMA) deployed to the VMs and Arc-enabled on-premises servers, configured with Data Collection Rules (DCRs) to send data to a Log Analytics
Application Insights SDK integrated at the operating system level for collecting infrastructure performance telemetry from each server
Azure Monitor Diagnostic Settings on each VM — routes platform logs to a Log Analytics workspace without requiring any agent installation
Azure Monitor Metrics Explorer — collects platform-level metrics from Azure resources directly with no agents needed on the VMs
questions.explanation: Azure Monitor Agent (AMA) is the modern unified agent replacing the legacy Log Analytics Agent (MMA) and Diagnostics Agent. It uses Data Collection Rules (DCRs) to define which data sources to collect (Windows Event Logs, Syslog, performance counters, custom text logs) and which workspace(s) to send data to. AMA works on Azure VMs, on-premises servers (via Azure Arc), and multi-cloud VMs. Platform metrics don't require an agent but cannot collect OS-level custom counters or application logs.

questions.question: An architect is designing a resource management strategy for a large organization with 3 business units, each with Dev/Test/Prod environments. They need separate billing, access isolation, and policy enforcement per environment. What structure best reflects this?
options: One subscription for all environments with resource groups per business unit and environment
An Azure Tenant per business unit with cross-tenant subscriptions for shared services
One subscription per environment type (Dev subscription, Test subscription, Prod subscription) for all business units
A management group hierarchy: Root → Business Unit MGs → Environment MGs.
questions.explanation: AZ-305 best practice for enterprise-scale: Management Groups provide policy/RBAC inheritance hierarchy. Separate subscriptions per BU×Environment provide billing isolation (each subscription has its own cost view), resource quota isolation, and a strong blast radius boundary. Policies assigned at the Environment MG (e.g., no public IPs in Prod) cascade to all BU Prod subscriptions automatically. One subscription for all environments creates governance and billing challenges. Multiple tenants add identity complexity without proportional benefit. with one subscription per business unit × environment combination (9 subscriptions total), policies and RBAC assigned at MG level

questions.question: A company needs to provide developers with self-service access to pre-approved Azure environments (specific VM sizes, approved images, region restrictions) without granting them broad subscription permissions. Which Azure service supports this governance pattern?
options: Azure Managed Applications published to an internal Service Catalog, allowing developers to deploy pre-approved packages from a
Azure Policy with 'allowed VM SKU' definitions and an approved image list applied to the developer subscription
Azure Blueprints assignments that deploy approved environments as reusable packages for each developer team
Azure Resource Manager templates published in a Git repo and deployed by a central operations team on demand
questions.explanation: Azure Managed Applications published to a Service Catalog allow operators to define pre-approved resource packages (VMs with specific SKUs, approved OS images, networking configurations) that developers can deploy from the Azure portal without seeing the underlying ARM templates or having broad RBAC permissions. The managed resource group is owned by the publisher, ensuring approved configurations. Blueprints are for subscription-level governance scaffolding, not per-developer self-service deployments.

questions.question: An architect needs to design a solution where no single person can approve their own access to sensitive resources. All privileged role activations must require approval from a second person and generate an audit log. Which Azure feature provides this?
options: Azure AD Access Reviews scheduled monthly to detect and revoke unauthorized privileged role assignments after the fact
Azure AD Privileged Identity Management (PIM) configured with eligible role assignments and an approval workflow before activation
Azure RBAC deny assignments scoped to each privileged role to block users from approving their own access requests
Azure AD Conditional Access policies with role-based assignment conditions and a sign-in risk approval flow
questions.explanation: PIM eligible assignments require users to activate the role (not permanently assigned) and can be configured to require multi-person approval before activation. The approver receives a notification, reviews the business justification, and approves or denies. All activation requests, approvals, and denials are logged in Azure AD audit logs. Access Reviews verify existing assignments but don't enforce real-time approval workflows for new activations.

questions.question: A company wants to receive proactive alerts when their Azure costs exceed $10,000 in a given month, and automatically suspend non-critical development VMs when spending reaches 90% of the budget. Which Azure feature enables both of these?
options: Azure Monitor metric alerts on billing metrics with Logic App workflows for VM management
Azure Advisor cost recommendations with automated remediation enabled
Azure Cost Management + Billing budget with action groups
Azure Policy with cost-based deny effects that prevent new resource creation above budget
questions.explanation: Azure Cost Management budgets allow you to set monthly spending thresholds with alert thresholds at multiple percentages (e.g., 80% and 90% of budget). At 90%, an action group can trigger an Azure Automation Runbook or Logic App that stops the development VMs. Email alerts notify cost owners at any threshold. Azure Advisor provides recommendations but not automated enforcement. Azure Policy cannot enforce budget-based restrictions.

questions.question: A solutions architect must ensure that all resource groups in a production subscription have specific tags (CostCenter, Owner, Environment) applied at the time of creation. Resources without these tags must not be created. Which Azure Policy effect enforces this?
options: Audit — logs non-compliant resources to the compliance dashboard
Modify — adds missing tags automatically but still allows creation with remediation tasks
Append — automatically adds missing tags with default values without blocking creation
Deny — rejects the deployment if required tags are missing
questions.explanation: The Deny policy effect is evaluated at request time and rejects the deployment if the conditions are met (required tags missing). Audit logs non-compliance but doesn't prevent it. Append adds fields to requests (e.g., can add tags if not provided, but cannot enforce specific non-empty values). Modify is used with remediation tasks to update existing resources but doesn't block new deployments. For mandatory tag enforcement at creation time, Deny is the correct effect.

questions.question: An architect needs to design a solution to prevent accidental deletion of a critical Azure SQL Database. Even subscription owners should not be able to delete it without explicit action. Which control achieves this?
options: Apply a CanNotDelete resource lock to the Azure SQL Database
Assign a custom RBAC role definition that denies the Microsoft.Sql/servers/databases/delete action to every user in the subscription
Enable Azure Backup for the database with immutable vault settings configured to retain backups beyond the deletion window
Apply a ReadOnly resource lock to the Azure SQL Database to prevent all modifications including any delete operations
questions.explanation: Resource locks override RBAC — even subscription Owners cannot perform the locked action without first removing the lock. CanNotDelete allows read and modify operations but blocks delete. ReadOnly blocks ALL writes including beneficial operations like scaling, failover, and configuration changes — too restrictive for a production database. RBAC deny assignments could work but cannot block subscription Owners who have the ability to modify RBAC. Backup provides recovery but doesn't prevent deletion.

questions.question: A solutions architect is designing a monitoring strategy. The application team needs to detect performance regressions in a .NET web application running on Azure App Service, including dependency call durations, exception rates, and user session tracking. Which monitoring solution is most appropriate?
options: Azure Network Watcher with packet capture and latency analysis on the inbound HTTP traffic to the App Service plan
Azure Monitor platform metrics for App Service — tracks CPU, memory consumption, and requests per second at the plan level
Application Insights enabled on the App Service for distributed request tracing, dependency timings, exception telemetry, and user-session
Log Analytics workspace with custom KQL queries running over IIS access logs streamed from the App Service file system
questions.explanation: Application Insights is the Azure APM (Application Performance Monitoring) service purpose-built for application-level telemetry. It captures HTTP request/response telemetry, dependency call durations (SQL, HTTP, Service Bus), exceptions and stack traces, custom events/metrics, user sessions (via JavaScript SDK), and availability tests. It integrates with distributed tracing (correlation IDs across microservices). Platform metrics only cover infrastructure. Log Analytics requires custom parsing. Network Watcher focuses on network-layer diagnostics.

questions.question: A company has a requirement to store Azure Activity Logs and Azure AD Sign-In Logs for 2 years for compliance purposes. The data must be queryable. Which design achieves this cost-effectively?
options: Configure Diagnostic Settings to route logs to Azure Storage (Archive tier) for long-term cheap retention
Configure Diagnostic Settings to route logs to a Log Analytics workspace with a 2-year retention period set
Export logs to Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 and use Azure Synapse Analytics for queries
Enable Microsoft Sentinel with a 2-year data retention policy — Sentinel indexes all logs for querying
questions.explanation: The cost-effective two-tier pattern: Log Analytics for active querying (90-day hot retention, after which logs are archived automatically) with logs also sent to Azure Storage (cool/archive tier) for compliance retention at low cost (~$0.002/GB/month for archive vs ~$2-3/GB/month for Log Analytics ingestion). Log Analytics workspace retention beyond 90 days incurs significant costs. This dual-destination approach via Diagnostic Settings is the AZ-305-recommended pattern for cost-optimized compliance logging. also stream to a Log Analytics workspace with 90-day retention for active analysis

questions.question: An architect is designing a BCDR solution for an on-premises application that must failover to Azure within 4 hours (RTO) and lose no more than 1 hour of data (RPO). The application runs on VMware VMs. Which Azure service meets these requirements?
options: Azure VMware Solution (AVS) with stretched clusters between the on-premises datacenter and the Azure environment for unified vSphere management
Azure Migrate Server Migration to convert the VMware VMs into Azure native VMs, then configure availability sets in the destination region
Azure Site Recovery (ASR) replicating the VMware VMs to Azure with continuous replication, recovery plans, and automated failover orchestration
Azure Backup with the MARS agent on each VMware VM scheduled for hourly backups and cross-region restore on disaster
questions.explanation: Azure Site Recovery provides continuous replication of VMware VMs to Azure with RPO as low as 15 seconds for Hyper-V and 5 minutes for VMware VMs using agentless replication. Automated recovery plans can failover hundreds of VMs in sequence, meeting a 4-hour RTO. Azure Backup provides scheduled snapshots (not continuous replication) and cannot meet 1-hour RPO reliably. Azure Migrate is a one-time migration tool, not a BCDR solution. AVS is a full VMware environment in Azure, overengineered for this requirement.

questions.question: A solutions architect needs to design high availability for an Azure SQL Database supporting a mission-critical application with an RTO of less than 30 seconds and an RPO of near-zero. What configuration achieves this?
options: Azure SQL Database General Purpose tier with Point-in-Time Restore configured at 1-minute granularity for the database backups
Azure SQL Database Hyperscale tier with distributed read replicas serving zero-RPO reads to the application during failover events
Azure SQL Database with Active Geo-Replication that synchronously replicates the primary to a secondary database in a paired region
Azure SQL Database Business Critical tier with Auto-Failover Groups providing sub-second local HA and automatic cross-region failover
questions.explanation: Business Critical tier uses an Always On availability group with 3-4 replicas in the same region, providing 99.995% SLA (< 26 min downtime/year) and sub-second failover. Auto-Failover Groups extend this to cross-region with configurable failover policies. Active Geo-Replication is ASYNCHRONOUS — it has potential data loss. Point-in-Time Restore is a recovery mechanism, not a HA mechanism (RTO is minutes to hours). Hyperscale read replicas are for scale-out reads, not HA failover. provides synchronous replication within the primary region (Business Critical SLA 99.995%) and automatic failover with data loss < 5 seconds

questions.question: An architect must ensure that Azure Virtual Machine Scale Sets (VMSS) hosting a stateless web application remain available if a single Azure datacenter fails. The application requires minimum 3 healthy instances at all times. How should the VMSS be configured?
options: Deploy two separate VMSS in two different regions and use Azure Traffic Manager for DNS failover
Deploy the VMSS in a single region with an Availability Set and 3 fault domains
Deploy the VMSS across 3 Availability Zones with a zone-redundant load balancer and set minimum
Deploy the VMSS with a Premium SSD managed disk for high availability
questions.explanation: Availability Zones are physically separate datacenters within a region with independent power, cooling, and networking. Deploying across 3 AZs means the VMSS survives a complete datacenter failure with instances in the other 2 AZs still serving traffic. The zone-redundant load balancer distributes traffic across all AZs. A minimum of 3 instances means at least 1 per zone. Availability Sets protect against rack/update domain failures within a single datacenter — not datacenter-level failures.

questions.question: A company needs to replicate an Azure SQL Database to a secondary region for disaster recovery. In the event of a regional outage, the failover should happen automatically without manual intervention. Which feature provides automatic cross-region failover?
options: Active Geo-Replication using the Failover Groups REST API to trigger manual failover after detecting a primary region outage
Azure Database for PostgreSQL with geo-redundant backups and geo-restore initiated by an Azure Automation runbook on alert
Auto-Failover Groups configured on the SQL logical server with a read-write listener that fails over automatically after the grace period
Azure SQL Managed Instance cross-instance failover in the Business Critical tier with manual region promotion via the portal
questions.explanation: Auto-Failover Groups are an abstraction on top of Active Geo-Replication that provide: a read-write listener DNS name (always points to primary), a read-only listener (points to secondary), automatic failover triggered after a configurable grace period (default 1 hour), and automatic DNS update during failover so applications reconnect transparently. Active Geo-Replication requires manual failover. Geo-restore is a backup restore operation (hours RTO). SQL Managed Instance failover groups exist but the question asks about SQL Database.

questions.question: An architect needs to design a backup strategy for 200 Azure VMs across 5 subscriptions, ensuring all VMs are backed up daily with 30-day retention. A central team must be able to monitor backup compliance from a single dashboard. What is the recommended design?
options: Deploy a third-party backup solution from the Azure Marketplace that supports multi-subscription policy management and dashboards
Create a Recovery Services Vault in each of the 5 subscriptions and configure individual VM backup policies on each vault separately
Enable Azure Snapshot Manager in Azure Monitor to schedule managed-disk snapshots across the subscriptions on a daily cadence
Use Azure Backup Center with an Azure Policy assignment that enforces a daily backup policy with 30-day retention on all VMs across the vaults
questions.explanation: Azure Backup Center is the unified management portal for all Azure Backup workloads across subscriptions, regions, and vault types. Combined with Azure Policy (built-in 'Configure backup on VMs with a given tag' policy), you can automatically enroll new VMs into backup, enforce retention policies, and monitor compliance status from a single pane. Recovery Services Vaults are still per-region/subscription but managed centrally. Backup Center provides cross-subscription reporting, compliance, and job monitoring dashboards.

questions.question: A company is designing its Azure storage strategy. Large files (video content, 50-500 GB each) will be uploaded once and accessed frequently for the first 30 days, rarely for the next 60 days, then almost never after 90 days. What lifecycle management policy minimizes cost?
options: Store all files in the Hot tier permanently and have an operations team manually move them to Cool after 30 days each cycle
Store the videos in Premium block blob for the fastest initial access, then delete them after 90 days when access drops off
Use Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 with auto-tiering enabled on the container holding the large video binary objects
Configure a Blob lifecycle management policy that transitions blobs to Cool at 30 days and to Archive at 90 days for cheap retention
questions.explanation: Azure Blob Storage lifecycle management policies automate tier transitions based on last-modified time. The cost tiers (Hot > Cool > Cold > Archive) allow optimizing cost vs access latency. For this pattern: Hot (30 days, frequent access), Cool (30-90 days, infrequent), Archive (90+ days, near-zero access). Archive is the cheapest tier (~$0.00099/GB/month) but has rehydration latency (hours). Lifecycle policies run daily and transition blobs automatically, eliminating manual operations.

questions.question: A company requires a relational database solution that supports elastic scaling of compute independently of storage, can pause compute when not in use (dev/test scenarios), and provides per-second billing. Which Azure SQL offering fits?
options: Azure SQL Database Serverless compute tier with auto-pause on inactivity, auto-resume on connection, and per-second billing of active compute
Azure SQL Database Hyperscale tier configured with zero replicas for dev/test scenarios so unused replicas do not incur cost
Azure SQL Managed Instance General Purpose tier with the serverless compute add-on for dev/test elasticity and pause-on-idle
Azure SQL Database Business Critical tier paired with auto-scaling groups that downsize the SKU during off-hours
questions.explanation: Azure SQL Database Serverless is purpose-built for intermittent, unpredictable usage patterns. It auto-scales compute vCores between a configured min and max based on workload, auto-pauses after a configurable inactivity period (minimum 60 minutes), and auto-resumes when a connection arrives (with a brief cold-start delay). Billing is per-second for active compute, plus per-GB for storage. This makes it ideal for dev/test databases that are idle nights and weekends. Business Critical and Managed Instance don't support auto-pause.

questions.question: An architect needs to choose a NoSQL database for a global e-commerce application that processes 1 million product catalog reads per second with single-digit millisecond latency. The data model is simple key-value lookups on product ID. Which Azure database service is most appropriate?
options: Azure Table Storage — a simple NoSQL key-value store at lower cost than Cosmos DB but with weaker latency SLAs
Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL with multi-region writes, autoscale RU/s, and a single-digit millisecond P99 read SLA
Azure SQL Database Business Critical tier with In-Memory OLTP tables tuned for high-throughput point reads
Azure Cache for Redis Premium as the primary catalog store with write-through replication back to Azure SQL
questions.explanation: Azure Cosmos DB is designed for planet-scale NoSQL with: single-digit millisecond read/write latency at the 99th percentile, automatic multi-region distribution with configurable consistency levels, elastic throughput scaling (Request Units, auto-scale), and 99.999% SLA for multi-region deployments. For 1M reads/second globally, Cosmos DB handles this natively. Azure Table Storage shares the Cosmos DB Table API but has lower SLAs and feature constraints. Redis is an in-memory cache (not a primary database). SQL with in-memory OLTP is still relational and has scaling limits.

questions.question: A retail company needs to ingest 50,000 IoT device events per second from sensors, transform the data, and load it into Azure Synapse Analytics for business intelligence reporting every 15 minutes. Which data pipeline architecture is appropriate?
options: Azure IoT Hub → Stream Analytics with tumbling-window transforms → ADLS Gen2 landing zone → Synapse pipelines for BI
Azure Event Hubs → Azure Functions for event-by-event processing → Cosmos DB → Azure Synapse Link for BI dashboards
Azure Event Grid → Azure Blob Storage → Azure Data Factory copy activity for periodic batch loading into Synapse
Azure IoT Hub → Azure Logic Apps for transformation → Azure SQL Database → Power BI Direct Query reports
questions.explanation: The standard IoT analytics pattern on Azure: IoT Hub ingests device telemetry at scale (supports millions of devices), Stream Analytics provides real-time SQL-like transformations and windowing functions, ADLS Gen2 acts as the data lake landing zone, and Synapse Analytics pipelines (or Synapse Link) enable BI workloads. Stream Analytics supports 50K events/second and outputs to ADLS with time-based tumbling windows (15 min = perfect match). Logic Apps are for orchestration, not high-throughput stream processing. Event Grid is for event routing, not stream processing.

questions.question: A company wants to run batch machine learning training jobs that require thousands of CPU cores for 4-hour windows, twice a week. After the jobs complete, no compute should be running. What Azure compute solution minimizes cost?
options: Azure Machine Learning compute clusters configured with min nodes = 0 and max nodes set to the desired CPU core scale
Azure Virtual Machine Scale Sets with a scheduled autoscale rule scaling instance count to 0 outside the job windows
Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) with the cluster autoscaler set to scale up to thousands of nodes during job runs
Azure Batch pools with auto-scale formulas and Spot/low-priority VMs to provision and tear down nodes per HPC job
questions.explanation: Azure Batch is specifically designed for large-scale parallel and HPC batch workloads. It manages pools of VMs, job scheduling, task distribution, and automatic scale-to-zero when idle. You only pay for VMs while they're running the batch job. Batch supports spot/low-priority VMs (60-90% discount) for further cost reduction. AML compute clusters also work but add ML-specific overhead. VMSS with scheduled scaling requires management. AKS adds Kubernetes overhead inappropriate for simple HPC batch workloads.

questions.question: An architect needs to host a containerized microservices application with 20 services. Some services need to scale to hundreds of instances under load, while others run 1-2 instances constantly. The team wants minimal Kubernetes management overhead. What is the recommended compute platform?
options: Azure Container Instances (ACI) hosting all 20 services as serverless containers billed per second of execution
Azure Functions on a consumption plan for all 20 microservices so each scales to zero when idle and per request otherwise
Azure App Service Premium plans for every service with built-in autoscaling and no Kubernetes knowledge required by the team
Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) with HPA and KEDA for per-service scaling, plus a managed control plane for low Kubernetes overhead
questions.explanation: AKS is the recommended platform for containerized microservices requiring mixed scaling patterns. AKS manages the Kubernetes control plane (Azure pays for masters), leaving only node pool management. KEDA (Kubernetes Event-driven Autoscaling) enables scale-to-zero for idle services. The cluster autoscaler handles node-level scaling. Services needing hundreds of instances use Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) with appropriate resource requests. ACI is for simple on-demand containers, not long-running microservices. App Service doesn't support container orchestration at this complexity.

questions.question: A company is migrating a monolithic .NET Framework 4.8 application to Azure. The application cannot be refactored and requires full IIS control, custom GAC assemblies, and Windows Registry access. Which compute option is appropriate?
options: Azure Container Instances running a Windows Server Core container image with IIS pre-installed in the image
Azure App Service (Windows) — managed PaaS with hosted IIS but restricted Registry and GAC access at the OS level
Azure Virtual Machines running Windows Server with full IIS, GAC, and Registry access for legacy lift-and-shift workloads
Azure Functions on the .NET Framework runtime with custom in-process bindings for COM+ component integration
questions.explanation: When an application requires deep OS-level customization (Windows Registry, GAC, specific IIS module configuration, COM+ components), a Virtual Machine (IaaS) is the appropriate lift-and-shift target. Azure App Service has Windows IIS support but restricts Registry and GAC access. Azure Functions requires refactoring to serverless. Windows containers support GAC but not all Registry paths and COM+ scenarios. The AZ-305 approach: migrate first to IaaS (full compatibility), then modernize to PaaS progressively if feasible.

questions.question: An architect must design a network topology for Azure where all traffic between spoke VNets must flow through a central hub that contains shared security appliances (next-gen firewall, IDS/IPS). New spoke VNets should connect with minimal configuration. What network topology achieves this?
options: Classic hub-and-spoke VNet peering with User Defined Routes on every spoke forcing inter-spoke traffic through the hub NVA
Azure Virtual WAN with a Secured Virtual Hub running Azure Firewall, with intent-based routing applied to all spoke connections
Site-to-site VPN connections from each spoke VNet to the hub VNet using a centralized VPN Gateway as the transit point
Full mesh VNet peering between all spoke VNets so traffic flows directly between spokes without any central transit
questions.explanation: Azure Virtual WAN Secured Virtual Hub integrates Azure Firewall (or third-party NVAs via NVA infrastructure) directly into the hub and uses intent-based routing to automatically route all inter-spoke and branch traffic through the firewall. New spokes connect to the vWAN hub with minimal configuration and inherit routing automatically. Classic hub-and-spoke with UDRs works but requires manual UDR management on every spoke as new spokes are added. Full mesh doesn't route through a central security point. VPN for VNet-to-VNet adds unnecessary complexity.

questions.question: A solutions architect must design connectivity from an on-premises datacenter to Azure with guaranteed bandwidth, low latency, and consistent throughput for a financial services application transferring large data sets. Which connectivity option is most appropriate?
options: Site-to-site IPsec VPN over the public internet — cost-effective with AES-256 encryption and BGP route exchange
Azure Virtual WAN with point-to-site VPN gateways for all on-premises users connecting from the corporate network
Azure ExpressRoute Direct with Global Reach providing 100 Gbps datacenter-to-datacenter private connectivity
Azure ExpressRoute with a dedicated private circuit through a connectivity provider for SLA-backed bandwidth and latency
questions.explanation: ExpressRoute provides a private, dedicated connection from on-premises to Azure via a connectivity provider, avoiding the public internet entirely. It offers: SLA-backed bandwidth from 50 Mbps to 10 Gbps (100 Gbps with ExpressRoute Direct), consistent latency, and private peering to Azure VNets. Financial services applications with large data transfers need deterministic throughput — internet-based VPN has variable latency and bandwidth. ExpressRoute Direct is for organizations requiring 100 Gbps direct connectivity, which is over-specified here.

questions.question: A global e-commerce company needs to route user traffic to the nearest Azure region to minimize latency. The solution must also perform health checks and automatically route around a failed region. Which Azure service provides this?
options: Azure Application Gateway with multi-region backend pools and cross-region health probes for layer-7 routing
Azure Traffic Manager — DNS-based global routing with Performance/Geographic/Weighted methods and endpoint health monitoring
Azure Front Door — global application delivery platform with anycast routing, integrated WAF, and CDN caching
Azure Load Balancer Standard with cross-region frontend IP and health probes configured against each regional pool
questions.explanation: Azure Traffic Manager is a DNS-based global traffic manager. With the Performance routing method, it directs users to the endpoint with the lowest latency (measured from Azure's distributed monitoring infrastructure). Health probes automatically remove failed endpoints from DNS responses within the configured TTL. Azure Front Door is also valid for global routing with lower latency (anycast, TCP connection reuse), but Traffic Manager is the classic answer for multi-region DNS-level load balancing. The AZ-305 exam specifically tests Traffic Manager routing methods.

questions.question: A company has deployed an Azure Application Gateway with WAF for their web application. The security team wants to terminate TLS at the Application Gateway and encrypt the connection between the gateway and backend web servers (end-to-end SSL). How should this be configured?
options: Configure HTTPS backend settings on the Application Gateway and upload the trusted root CA of the backend server certificate
Place Azure API Management in front of the Application Gateway to handle the backend TLS handshake on its behalf
Use Azure Front Door with end-to-end encryption instead since Application Gateway does not support HTTPS to backends
Configure HTTP backend settings on the Application Gateway since gateway-to-backend traffic is encrypted automatically
questions.explanation: Application Gateway supports end-to-end SSL by: (1) terminating the client TLS at the frontend listener with a public certificate, (2) re-encrypting the connection to backend servers using backend HTTPS settings with the backend server's certificate (or trusted root CA). You upload the root certificate of the CA that signed the backend certificate. This ensures the full connection is encrypted even between the gateway and internal backend VMs, satisfying end-to-end encryption requirements.

questions.question: An architect is designing a network security strategy for an Azure environment. The requirement is to block all internet egress traffic from VMs and only allow outbound traffic to specific service endpoints (Azure Storage and Azure SQL). How should this be implemented?
options: Configure Azure Firewall with application rules allowing outbound traffic only to Azure Storage and SQL public IP ranges
Deploy Private Endpoints for Storage and SQL with a UDR sending 0.0.0.0/0 to an NVA that blocks internet but permits the private IPs
Use NSG outbound rules denying internet traffic plus rules allowing the Storage and Sql service tags, with VNet Service Endpoints enabled
Deploy an Azure NAT Gateway on the subnet and configure route tables that drop 0.0.0.0/0 to block internet egress entirely
questions.explanation: NSG outbound rules with service tags allow traffic to 'Storage.EastUS' and 'Sql.EastUS' service tag ranges, then deny all internet traffic (0.0.0.0/0). VNet Service Endpoints for Storage and SQL ensure traffic from the VNet to these services routes through the Azure backbone (not the internet) and the Storage/SQL firewall can restrict access to the specific VNet subnet. This is simpler and cheaper than Azure Firewall for service-specific egress control. Private Endpoints also work but are more complex and costly.

questions.question: A company is planning to migrate 200 on-premises servers to Azure. The migration team needs to discover and assess all servers (VMware, physical, Hyper-V) to understand dependencies, right-size VM SKUs in Azure, and estimate monthly costs before migrating. Which Azure service provides this assessment capability?
options: Azure Site Recovery configured with pre-migration assessment reports for the on-premises VMware and Hyper-V hosts
Azure Monitor with the Dependency Map (VM Insights) feature to discover relationships between the on-premises servers
Azure Migrate with the Discovery and Assessment tool — appliance-based discovery, right-sizing, dependency analysis, and cost estimates
Azure Cost Management + Billing combined with right-sizing recommendations from Azure Advisor for the migration estimate
questions.explanation: Azure Migrate is the centralized hub for Azure migration. The Discovery and Assessment project deploys a lightweight appliance (on-premises VM) that discovers VMware, Hyper-V, or physical servers without requiring agents for basic discovery. It provides right-sized Azure VM SKU recommendations based on actual performance data, dependency mapping (with the Dependency Agent for detailed maps), monthly cost estimates for compute and storage, and readiness assessment for Azure. ASR is a migration/replication tool, not an assessment tool.

questions.question: An architect needs to migrate a 10 TB on-premises SQL Server database to Azure SQL Managed Instance with minimal downtime. The migration must not impact production during business hours. Which service and approach achieves this?
options: Detach the database MDF/LDF files, upload them to Azure Blob Storage, then attach them to the SQL Managed Instance
Use SQL Server transactional replication to replicate all databases to the SQL Managed Instance, then switch application connection strings
Azure Database Migration Service in online migration mode with continuous transaction log sync and a brief cutover at the end
Azure Backup for SQL Server with the workload-aware extension, then restore the backups into the SQL Managed Instance
questions.explanation: Azure Database Migration Service (DMS) in online mode provides continuous data replication: the initial full load is followed by continuous incremental sync of transaction log changes. Production writes to the source SQL Server during the migration, and DMS keeps the target SQL MI synchronized. When ready to cut over, you stop applications briefly, let DMS sync the final changes, then switch connection strings. This minimizes downtime to just the final cutover window (typically minutes). Backup/restore and file attach are offline migration methods requiring full downtime.

questions.question: A company needs to move 500 TB of data from on-premises NAS to Azure Blob Storage. The internet connection is only 100 Mbps and encrypting 500 TB over the internet would take 46+ days. Which Azure data transfer service eliminates this constraint?
options: Azure Data Factory with parallel self-hosted integration runtimes copying the NAS data over the existing internet circuit
Azure Import/Export service — ship customer-supplied physical hard drives to an Azure datacenter for direct ingestion
Azure ExpressRoute with a newly provisioned 10 Gbps circuit dedicated to the bulk migration data transfer window
Azure Data Box Heavy — a physical appliance shipped to the customer site, loaded with the data, and returned to Azure
questions.explanation: Azure Data Box is Microsoft's offline data transfer solution for large datasets. The Data Box holds 80 TB usable (100 TB raw) per unit, uses AES-256 encryption, and can be ordered in quantities. For 500 TB, use Data Box Heavy (770 TB usable) or multiple Data Box units. The physical device ships to your datacenter, you load data locally at network/disk speed (bypassing internet bandwidth), then ship it back to Azure. Microsoft uploads the data and sends you a certificate of data erasure. ExpressRoute requires 2-3 months procurement. Data Factory requires available bandwidth.

questions.question: An e-commerce application experiences Black Friday spikes of 100x normal traffic. The application is hosted on Azure App Service. The architect wants the application to scale out automatically based on HTTP request queue length, not just CPU. Which autoscaling approach enables custom metric scaling?
options: Azure App Service automatic scaling (preview) based on the average HTTP request latency metric for the plan
Configure App Service autoscale rules on the HttpQueueLength metric — scale out when > 10, scale in when < 1
Use Azure Traffic Manager to distribute traffic across multiple App Service plans whenever the load increases sharply
Deploy Azure Front Door with origin groups to absorb traffic spikes at the edge tier before requests reach App Service
questions.explanation: Azure App Service exposes custom metrics including HttpQueueLength (number of requests waiting in the HTTP queue) that can trigger autoscale rules. This metric is more relevant for queue-based bottlenecks than CPU — a healthy app might have low CPU but a growing HTTP queue if I/O-bound. Autoscale rules: scale out when HttpQueueLength > 10 (add instances), scale in when < 1 (remove instances). This provides more responsive scaling than CPU for web workloads. Traffic Manager is DNS-level, not application-level autoscaling.

questions.question: A solutions architect needs to design an API layer for a microservices application. The API must support rate limiting, request/response transformation, authentication (JWT validation), developer portal for API documentation, and monetization through subscription keys. Which Azure service provides all of these capabilities?
options: Azure API Management with inbound/outbound policies, JWT validation, a developer portal, and product subscription keys for monetization
Azure Application Gateway with the WAF SKU configured for API security, URL-based routing, and header rewrite rules
Azure Functions with custom middleware that implements rate limiting, JWT validation, and request transformation per endpoint
Azure Front Door with the Rules Engine for API routing, WAF protection, and edge-based authentication enforcement
questions.explanation: Azure API Management is specifically designed as a full-lifecycle API management platform. Key features: Inbound/outbound policies (rate limiting, IP filtering, JWT validation, header transformation), OAuth2/OpenID Connect integration, developer portal (auto-generated API documentation, subscription management), product tiers with subscription keys for monetization, built-in analytics, and backend load balancing. Application Gateway and Front Door are network-layer load balancers without API management capabilities. Azure Functions require building all cross-cutting concerns from scratch.

questions.question: An architect is designing a solution for an application that processes financial transactions. Each transaction must be processed exactly once, in order, and failures must be retried without duplicate processing. Which messaging pattern is most appropriate?
options: Azure Event Hubs for real-time transaction streaming with multiple consumer groups reading the same partition stream
Azure Storage Queue with at-least-once delivery and application-level deduplication logic implemented in each consumer
Azure Service Bus Queues with message sessions for FIFO ordering per session key, plus duplicate detection and a dead-letter queue
Azure Event Grid for event-driven transaction processing with built-in retry policies and per-subscriber dead-lettering
questions.explanation: Service Bus Queues provide exactly-once, ordered processing through: (1) Message Sessions — enables FIFO ordering per session key (e.g., account ID), ensuring transactions for the same account are processed in order, (2) Duplicate detection — if a message is resent with the same MessageId within a configurable window, Service Bus discards the duplicate, (3) Dead-letter queue (DLQ) for messages that fail after max retries. Event Hubs is optimized for high-throughput telemetry streaming, not reliable ordered business transactions. Storage Queue has no ordering guarantee and no duplicate detection.

questions.question: A developer team wants to deploy a web application using containers to Azure with no Kubernetes management overhead, automatic HTTPS, built-in scale-to-zero, and support for sidecar containers. Which Azure service provides all of these?
options: Azure Container Apps — managed container PaaS with KEDA autoscale (including scale-to-zero), HTTPS ingress, and sidecar support
Azure Container Instances (ACI) — serverless containers with no cluster management and per-second billing on each container group
Azure App Service for Containers running a Docker image with built-in autoscaling and managed TLS via App Service plans
Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) with a serverless node pool using Virtual Nodes for burst capacity into ACI underneath
questions.explanation: Azure Container Apps is the modern PaaS for microservices containers without Kubernetes management. It provides: KEDA-based autoscaling including scale-to-zero, built-in HTTPS ingress with auto-managed TLS certificates, sidecar container support (Dapr integration), revision management for blue-green deployments, and support for event-driven architectures. ACI is for single containers without built-in HTTP ingress or KEDA scaling. App Service supports containers but doesn't support sidecars natively. AKS requires cluster management.

questions.question: A company processes 10 million Azure AD sign-in logs per day and needs to retain them for 90 days with the ability to query specific user sign-in events interactively. Log Analytics ingestion costs are a concern. Which cost-optimized design supports this?
options: Ingest all 10M daily sign-in logs into the standard Log Analytics Analytics-plan table at the workspace's normal ingestion price
Use Microsoft Sentinel on the Log Analytics workspace with a commitment tier purchased to obtain a volume ingestion discount
Archive the sign-in logs to Azure Storage cool tier and query them with a self-hosted ELK stack running on Azure VMs
Send the sign-in logs via Diagnostic Settings to a Log Analytics workspace using the Basic logs table for cheaper ingestion
questions.explanation: Azure Monitor Logs introduced Basic and Auxiliary log plans (alongside the standard Analytics plan). Basic plan: significantly lower ingestion cost (~$0.50/GB vs ~$2.30/GB for Analytics), 8-day interactive query retention, archival for up to 12 years. For Azure AD Sign-In Logs where you primarily need to search specific events (not complex analytics), the Basic plan delivers significant cost savings. Analytics plan provides full KQL capabilities but at higher cost. The AZ-305 cost optimization domain tests knowledge of log plan tiers.

questions.question: An organization must implement multi-region active-active deployment for a web application with shared state. Users must always be routed to the nearest healthy region, and sessions must be consistent across regions. Which Azure services form this architecture?
options: Azure Traffic Manager with Geographic routing; Azure SQL Database with Active Geo-Replication for read-only replicas in each region
Azure Front Door for global traffic routing with origin health probes; Azure Cosmos DB with multi-region writes for shared session state
Azure Load Balancer Standard (cross-region) with Azure Cache for Redis Premium geo-replication for cross-region session reads
Azure Application Gateway in each region behind Traffic Manager DNS; Azure SQL Database with Auto-Failover Groups for session data
questions.explanation: Azure Front Door provides global anycast routing to the nearest healthy region with sub-second health probe detection and automatic failover. For active-active with shared session state, Cosmos DB with multi-region write (also called multi-master) is the key: any region can write sessions, with automatic conflict resolution and replication to all regions. SQL Geo-Replication provides read-only secondaries — cannot write to secondaries in active-active. Redis geo-replication is asynchronous and doesn't support multi-master writes.

questions.question: A company's security team requires that all access to Azure Key Vault secrets from application VMs happens over private network paths — no public internet. The VMs are in an Azure VNet. Which network design achieves this?
options: Enable the Key Vault firewall and add the VNet subnet to the allowed Virtual Networks list using a Service Endpoint
Deploy Azure Firewall in the hub VNet and add the Key Vault FQDN to its allowed application rules collection
Configure NSG outbound rules on the application subnet to block all egress except traffic to Key Vault's public IPs
Deploy a Private Endpoint for the Key Vault in the application VNet, with a Private DNS Zone resolving the vault FQDN
questions.explanation: Private Endpoints create a private network interface with a private IP address within your VNet for the Key Vault. Azure Private DNS Zones override public DNS resolution so 'vault.vault.azure.net' resolves to the private IP instead of the public endpoint. All traffic from VMs to Key Vault flows through the VNet/backbone, never traversing the internet. Service Endpoints keep traffic on the backbone but the Key Vault endpoint is still a public IP from the VM's perspective — it doesn't provide full private connectivity for all scenarios. Private Endpoint is the recommended approach for strict private access requirements.

questions.question: A startup is designing its first Azure application — a web app with a REST API backend and a SQL database. The team has 2 developers and needs to be productive with minimal infrastructure management. The expected load is 100-500 users/day for the first 6 months. What is the most appropriate architecture?
options: Azure App Service Basic tier for the web app and API, Azure SQL Database S0 DTU tier, and Application Insights for monitoring
Azure Kubernetes Service with a managed node pool, an Ingress controller, and Azure SQL Database General Purpose backing it
Azure Virtual Machines for the API (Windows Server + IIS), Azure SQL Database Basic tier, and Azure Application Gateway in front
Azure Functions consumption plan for the API, Cosmos DB serverless for data, and Azure Static Web Apps for the frontend
questions.explanation: For a small team with minimal operations overhead and low initial load, PaaS services are ideal: App Service manages OS patching, scaling, and TLS; Azure SQL Database manages backup, patching, and HA. The Basic/Standard DTU tiers are cost-effective for 100-500 users/day. Application Insights provides out-of-the-box APM. This is the AZ-305 principle of 'right-sizing and right-tiering' — AKS is over-engineered for a 2-person startup. VMs add infrastructure management burden. Functions/Cosmos DB works but adds complexity when the team may not need it yet.

questions.question: An architect needs to design an Azure AD identity solution that allows external business partners to sign in using their own organizational credentials (Microsoft Entra ID, Google Workspace, or SAML IdP) to access a shared portal. Partner users should not have accounts created in the host directory. Which feature enables this?
options: Azure AD Connect configured to sync each partner's on-premises AD forest into the host directory as full users
Azure AD B2C with custom user flows for partner onboarding and a dedicated B2C tenant for the external identities
Azure AD External Identities B2B collaboration — partners sign in with their own IdP credentials and a guest object is created
Azure AD Domain Services to provide Kerberos authentication for the partner accounts within the host directory tenant
questions.explanation: Azure AD External Identities (B2B) allows external partners to use their existing credentials (Entra ID, Google, SAML/WS-Fed IdP, or Microsoft Account) to access shared applications. A lightweight guest object is created in the host directory representing the external identity, but the partner's password is never stored — authentication happens at the partner's IdP. The host admin can control access via Conditional Access, Entitlement Management, and Access Reviews. B2C is designed for consumer-facing apps where users create accounts. AD Connect syncs accounts, which would create full member accounts.

questions.question: A company needs to enforce a standard set of Azure resource configurations (resource groups, RBAC, policies, Log Analytics workspace) across every new subscription created in their organization. The configuration must be version-controlled and consistent. Which service automates this subscription-level baseline deployment?
options: Azure Blueprints — package ARM templates, policy assignments, role assignments, and resource groups as a versioned artifact assigned per subscription
Azure Resource Manager templates deployed manually to each newly created subscription by the platform engineering team on demand
Terraform automation triggered by an Azure DevOps pipeline that fires on the Microsoft.Subscription/subscriptionCreated event
Azure Policy initiatives assigned at the management group scope to configure resources within new subscriptions automatically
questions.explanation: Azure Blueprints are designed for subscription-level governance scaffolding. A blueprint definition packages: ARM templates (for resource creation), policy assignments (for governance), role assignments (for RBAC), and resource group creation — all as a single versioned artifact. When assigned to a subscription, it deploys all artifacts consistently. Blueprints track the assignment relationship, so blueprint changes can be pushed to all assigned subscriptions. Azure Policy only manages policy assignments, not resource creation. Terraform works but isn't a native Azure governance service tested on AZ-305.

questions.question: An architect needs to design a storage solution for a data science team. The team needs to store petabytes of raw CSV, Parquet, and JSON files in a hierarchical folder structure, with role-based access at both folder and file level. Query tools must be able to read files using standard tools. Which Azure storage service is most appropriate?
options: Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 with hierarchical namespace enabled, POSIX ACLs at file and folder level, and analytics-optimized throughput
Azure Managed Disks attached to a Linux VM exposing the data over NFS v4.1 to the data science team for shared filesystem access
Azure Files (SMB) with directory-level Azure RBAC for hierarchical folder access and share snapshots for the analytics team
Azure Blob Storage (flat namespace) with container-level RBAC for access control and a shared SAS URL per analyst
questions.explanation: Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 (ADLS Gen2) is Azure Blob Storage with hierarchical namespace (HNS) enabled. HNS provides: true directory operations (rename/delete are O(1) atomic operations, not O(n) copies), POSIX-compliant ACLs for file-and-folder-level access control (owner, group, other with rwx permissions), and 10x+ performance improvement for analytics operations. It supports Parquet/CSV/JSON natively and integrates with Azure Synapse, Databricks, and HDInsight. Flat-namespace Blob has no folder-level POSIX ACLs. Azure Files uses SMB, not optimized for analytics.

questions.question: A solutions architect must choose a database for storing user profiles in a social media application. User profiles have variable schemas (some users have optional fields, nested arrays of interests, and linked accounts). The application expects 100,000 reads/second with consistent single-digit millisecond latency. Which database is most appropriate?
options: Azure SQL Database with JSON columns and computed indexes for flexible schema support across the user profile records
Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL with auto-scale RU/s, document indexing, and a single-digit ms P99 read SLA backed by SLA
Azure Table Storage as a simple key-value store with flexible schema at lower cost than Cosmos DB or SQL options
Azure SQL Database Hyperscale tier configured with up to 4 read replicas to scale reads to 100K queries per second
questions.explanation: Variable-schema user profiles (nested arrays, optional fields, linked accounts) map naturally to a document model (JSON). Cosmos DB NoSQL API stores each user profile as a JSON document, supports nested structures natively without table joins, and scales to any throughput by provisioning Request Units (RUs) — auto-scale RU mode handles 100K reads/second without pre-provisioning. Single-digit ms P99 latency is a contractual SLA, not just a target. SQL Database JSON columns add relational overhead and don't scale horizontally. Table Storage lacks query flexibility for nested properties.

questions.question: An architect is designing a solution that will run thousands of short-lived (5-15 second) background tasks triggered by messages in an Azure Storage Queue. The code is simple, stateless, and must scale to zero when the queue is empty to minimize costs. What is the most cost-effective compute option?
options: Azure Functions on the consumption plan with a Storage Queue trigger — scales from 0 to hundreds of instances and bills per execution
Azure Kubernetes Service with KEDA queue-based autoscaling on a node pool sized for the peak per-task concurrency requirements
Azure Container Apps with the Storage Queue KEDA scaler attached to a single revision running the worker container image
Azure Logic Apps consumption plan with a Storage Queue trigger and a built-in retry policy for the per-message workflow
questions.explanation: Azure Functions consumption plan is purpose-built for this pattern: event-triggered, short-lived, stateless tasks. The Storage Queue trigger uses KEDA internally to scale from 0 to N instances based on queue depth (up to 200 concurrent function instances per plan). Billing is per 100ms execution units — with 5-15 second tasks, this is highly cost-effective. The first 1M executions per month are free. Scale-to-zero means no cost when the queue is empty. AKS and Container Apps add management overhead. Logic Apps are designed for workflow orchestration, not high-throughput message processing.

questions.question: A company uses Azure DevOps pipelines to deploy infrastructure and applications. The pipelines require access to Azure Key Vault secrets (API keys, certificates) during deployment. The best practice is to avoid storing secrets in pipeline variables or service connection credentials. How should the pipeline access secrets securely?
options: Store the secrets in Azure App Configuration and reference them as masked environment variables in each pipeline stage
Use an Azure DevOps variable group linked directly to Key Vault
Pass the secrets as base64-encoded parameters from a secure webhook trigger into the pipeline at queue time
Hardcode the secrets in the pipeline YAML and use Azure Repos branch access controls to restrict who can view the file
questions.explanation: Azure DevOps Variable Groups support direct Key Vault integration: the variable group is linked to a Key Vault and a service principal, and specified secrets are fetched directly from Key Vault at pipeline run time — they are never stored in Azure DevOps. Pipeline tasks use the variable group secrets as masked pipeline variables. The service principal used for Key Vault access needs Key Vault Secrets Get permissions. This pattern keeps secrets centralized in Key Vault with rotation, auditing, and access control managed there.

questions.question: An architect is designing a solution to process files uploaded to Azure Blob Storage — each new file must trigger an image resizing function within 30 seconds. The system processes 10,000 file uploads per hour. Which trigger type provides the most reliable near-real-time processing?
options: Azure Functions with a Timer trigger running every 30 seconds to enumerate the container looking for newly arrived blobs
Azure Functions triggered by Event Grid on the Microsoft.Storage.BlobCreated event from the storage account container
Azure Logic Apps with a Recurrence trigger checking the container for new blobs every minute and processing each batch
Azure Functions with the native Azure Blob Storage trigger — polls the container for new blobs on a built-in schedule
questions.explanation: Azure Blob Storage Trigger (native) uses polling, which can have 10-minute delays for large containers. The recommended pattern for near-real-time processing is using Azure Event Grid: Storage Blob Created events are delivered within milliseconds, and Event Grid triggers a Function directly. At 10,000 uploads/hour (~2.7/second), Event Grid handles this comfortably. The Event Grid subscription filters for blob.created events and routes them to the Function endpoint. This is the AZ-305-recommended pattern for event-driven blob processing.

questions.question: A company needs to deploy an application across multiple Azure regions for global availability. The application uses Azure Service Bus for messaging. The messaging layer must continue to work if an entire Azure region becomes unavailable. What feature provides this for Service Bus?
options: Service Bus Federation for active-active message replication across regions implemented with Azure Functions copying messages
Service Bus Premium tier with availability zones enabled — protects against datacenter failures within a single region
Azure Traffic Manager DNS routing across two independent Service Bus namespaces deployed in different paired regions
Service Bus Geo-Disaster Recovery — pairs a primary and secondary namespace with metadata sync and an alias connection string
questions.explanation: Service Bus Geo-Disaster Recovery pairs a primary namespace with a secondary namespace in a different region. It synchronizes entity metadata (queues, topics, subscriptions) but NOT message data — messages in flight are not replicated. On failover, the secondary becomes the new primary and the same alias connection string resolves to the secondary. Applications reconnect automatically via the alias. Availability Zones protect against datacenter failures within a region, not full regional outages. Federation does replicate messages but is more complex.

questions.question: A company's compliance team requires that ALL changes to Azure resources (creates, updates, deletes) in their production subscription be logged and retained for 1 year. The logs must be queryable. What is the correct configuration?
options: Configure a Diagnostic Setting at the subscription scope exporting Activity Logs to a Log Analytics workspace with 365-day retention
Deploy Microsoft Sentinel and connect the Azure Activity data connector — Sentinel applies 1-year retention to the workspace by default
Enable Azure Policy with the 'Audit if Activity Log is not retained' built-in initiative assigned at the subscription scope
Enable Defender for Cloud on the subscription — its activity logging feature retains all resource change events for one year
questions.explanation: Azure Activity Logs capture all control-plane operations (resource creates, updates, deletes, RBAC changes, policy assignments) for the subscription. By default they're retained 90 days. To retain for 1 year: create a Diagnostic Setting at the subscription scope to export Activity Logs to a Log Analytics workspace (configure 365-day retention) or Azure Storage. The workspace enables KQL querying. This is standard configuration — no additional services like Defender or Sentinel are required, though they may augment it.

questions.question: An architect needs to design a solution where an Azure Function needs to call multiple Azure services (Blob Storage, Cosmos DB, Key Vault) without storing any credentials or connection strings in the function's application settings. Which identity pattern is recommended?
options: Store the credentials encrypted in Azure Key Vault and configure the Function to fetch them via the Key Vault reference syntax in App Settings
Enable system-assigned Managed Identity on the Function and grant it the appropriate data-plane RBAC role on each target service
Create a service principal in Azure AD with certificates stored in Key Vault and use it for authentication from the Function
Store all connection strings in Azure App Configuration with access-key authentication and read them at Function startup
questions.explanation: Managed Identity eliminates credential management entirely — there are no secrets to store, rotate, or secure. The system-assigned MI is automatically created and bound to the Function lifecycle. Azure services that support Azure AD authentication (Blob Storage, Cosmos DB, Key Vault, Service Bus, Event Hubs, SQL Database) can authenticate the managed identity via RBAC or access policies. This is the #1 AZ-305 recommended pattern for Azure-to-Azure service authentication. Key Vault references (option D) still require an authentication credential for Key Vault itself.

questions.question: A company wants to build a serverless event-driven architecture where order placement events trigger inventory updates, billing, and notification workflows independently. If one downstream service is temporarily unavailable, the event must be retried without losing it. Which Azure messaging service is designed for this pattern?
options: Azure Event Grid — serverless event routing with at-least-once delivery, exponential retry, and dead-lettering per subscriber
Azure Storage Queue — simple queuing with at-least-once delivery for background job processing across multiple consumers
Azure Service Bus — reliable message queuing with competing consumers, ordered processing, and dead-letter queue support
Azure Event Hubs — high-throughput streaming for real-time analytics on order events using consumer groups per subscriber
questions.explanation: Azure Event Grid is purpose-built for event-driven pub/sub scenarios: publishers emit events (Order Placed), and multiple subscribers (inventory service, billing service, notification service) receive independent copies. Event Grid provides at-least-once delivery with built-in retry (exponential backoff, up to 24 hours), dead-lettering for undeliverable events, and subscriber isolation (one subscriber's failure doesn't affect others). Service Bus is for reliable ordered queue-based messaging (point-to-point or pub/sub with sessions). Event Hubs is for high-throughput telemetry streaming with consumer groups.

questions.question: A company needs to deploy a highly available web application in Azure with connection-based session affinity (sticky sessions) and SSL offloading. The web tier has 10 VMs in the same VNet. Which load balancer supports these requirements?
options: Azure Front Door — global anycast application delivery with SSL offloading and session affinity applied at the edge POPs
Azure Traffic Manager — DNS-based global load balancer with the Subnet routing method providing endpoint-affinity
Azure Load Balancer Standard — layer 4 load balancing with health probes but no SSL termination or cookie affinity
Azure Application Gateway — layer 7 load balancer with cookie-based session affinity, SSL offloading, and optional WAF
questions.explanation: Azure Application Gateway is a layer 7 (HTTP/HTTPS) load balancer. Key features for this scenario: Cookie-based affinity inserts a custom cookie on the first response, binding the client to a specific backend for subsequent requests (sticky sessions). SSL/TLS offloading terminates HTTPS at the gateway, allowing HTTP communication to backends (reducing backend CPU load). WAF can be added for web application protection. ALB Standard is layer 4 — it can do hash-based affinity (source IP) but not cookie-based, and doesn't terminate SSL. Traffic Manager is DNS-level (no sticky sessions within a region).

questions.question: An architect needs to design an Azure solution for running a legacy application that requires a Windows Server 2012 R2 environment. The company policy mandates that all Azure VMs must use the latest security updates. How should the patching strategy be designed?
options: Manual patching performed by the system administrators via RDP on each VM during a monthly maintenance window
Azure Update Manager (formerly Update Management Center) for centralized patch assessment and scheduled deployments
Azure Automation Hybrid Runbook Worker running custom patch scripts on each VM via PowerShell DSC compliance
Azure Guest OS automatic patching enabled on the VMs so Azure applies all available patches without explicit scheduling
questions.explanation: Azure Update Manager provides centralized patch management for Azure VMs and Arc-enabled servers. It assesses missing patches in real-time without deploying a management solution, creates patching schedules with maintenance windows to minimize disruption, supports reboot preferences, pre/post maintenance scripts, and cross-subscription multi-VM management from a single view. It supports Windows Server 2012 R2 through current versions. Guest OS automatic patching is limited to Azure-recommended patches and has limited schedule control — not suitable for controlled production environments.

questions.question: A company needs a storage solution for SMB file shares that Windows VMs access like traditional on-premises network drives. The solution must support Active Directory authentication for access control and provide 99.99% availability SLA. Which Azure service provides this?
options: Azure NetApp Files for enterprise NFS and SMB workloads with three performance tiers and dedicated capacity pools
Azure Disk Storage in shared-disk configuration backing a clustered Windows Server File Server failover instance
Azure Files Premium with the SMB 3.0 protocol, AD DS authentication, and ZRS for the 99.99% availability SLA
Azure Blob Storage with the NFS v3 protocol enabled for Windows VM access via the NFS client feature
questions.explanation: Azure Files provides fully managed SMB file shares in Azure. Premium tier with ZRS (Zone-Redundant Storage) provides 99.99% SLA. Azure AD Kerberos authentication (or on-premises AD DS integration) allows existing AD users/groups to access shares with their domain credentials — no separate user management. Windows VMs mount the share as a network drive using standard UNC paths. This is the recommended migration target for on-premises file servers. NetApp Files is for high-performance NFS/SMB but at significantly higher cost. Blob NFS is for Linux POSIX workloads.

questions.question: A solutions architect needs to design a globally distributed application that caches frequently read data to minimize database load. The cache must be highly available within a region and should share no single point of failure between cache and primary database. Which Azure caching solution supports replication within a region for HA?
options: Azure Cosmos DB integrated cache configured in front of the container for sub-millisecond cached reads of hot items
Azure Content Delivery Network for caching API responses at edge POPs globally with origin shielding to the database
Azure Table Storage with row-level caching enabled for frequently accessed records, fronted by an HTTP API layer
Azure Cache for Redis Standard or Premium tier with primary-replica replication, automatic failover, and a 99.9%+ SLA
questions.explanation: Azure Cache for Redis is the managed in-memory data store for caching, session storage, and message brokering. Standard tier provides a two-node primary-replica setup with automatic failover and 99.9% SLA. Premium tier adds clustering (multiple shards), persistence (RDB/AOF), and geo-replication for cross-region cache reads. This directly addresses the HA requirement within a region. CDN caches static content at edge, not application-layer cache. Table Storage is a persistent database, not a cache. Cosmos DB integrated cache is a feature for Cosmos DB itself, not a general-purpose caching layer.

questions.question: An architect is designing a network solution that requires Azure VMs in one VNet to communicate with services in a third-party SaaS provider's Azure VNet, without exposing traffic to the internet and without requiring VNet peering. What technology enables this?
options: Use Azure ExpressRoute Microsoft Peering to route traffic between the two VNets through the Microsoft global backbone
Deploy a Site-to-Site IPsec VPN tunnel between the company's VNet gateway and the SaaS provider's VNet gateway
Configure VNet peering directly between the company's VNet and the SaaS provider's VNet across the two tenants
The SaaS provider publishes a Private Link Service and the consumer creates a Private Endpoint in its own VNet
questions.explanation: Azure Private Link enables service providers to expose their services as Private Link Services. Consumers create a Private Endpoint in their own VNet, which receives a private IP in the consumer's address space. Traffic flows from the consumer VM → consumer VNet → Azure backbone → Private Link Service → provider VNet without VNet peering (no overlapping IP concerns), without internet exposure, and without the provider needing visibility into the consumer's network. This is the standard pattern for SaaS providers (including Microsoft PaaS services) and enterprise service sharing.

questions.question: An organization needs to implement an Azure governance model that assigns specific subscription management responsibilities to different teams: a Networking team that manages all virtual networks across subscriptions, a Security team that manages Azure Policy, and individual app teams that manage their own resource groups. What RBAC design achieves this?
options: Grant all three teams the Owner role at the root management group scope to maximize their day-to-day flexibility
Networking team: Network Contributor at the networking MG; Security team: Policy Contributor at root MG; App teams: Contributor on their RGs
Create a single shared service account with Owner permission at root and share its credentials between the three teams
Grant all teams Contributor at the subscription scope and use Azure Policy to restrict what each team can do per resource type
questions.explanation: AZ-305 governance best practice: assign RBAC at the lowest scope that meets requirements. Network Contributor at MG/subscription scope gives the networking team management rights over VNets without access to other resources. Policy Contributor at MG scope allows the security team to create/assign policies without infrastructure access. App team Contributor at resource group scope gives full resource management rights within their boundary without cross-team access. This implements separation of duties — each team has rights over their domain only. Owner at root MG is a massive security risk.

questions.question: A company is designing a solution for sharing large datasets between Azure Data Factory pipelines and Azure Machine Learning workspaces. The datasets are stored in Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2. Both services need read/write access without using storage account keys. What is the recommended identity pattern?
options: Enable system-assigned managed identities on both ADF and AML and grant each the Storage Blob Data Contributor role on the ADLS Gen2 account
Create a shared storage account key, store it in Azure Key Vault, and reference it from both Data Factory and Machine Learning
Use an Azure AD service principal per service with certificates stored in Key Vault for authentication to the storage account
Configure user-delegation SAS tokens with read/write permissions on the containers and renew them every 30 days for both services
questions.explanation: Managed Identities for Azure services (ADF, AML, AKS, Functions, etc.) eliminate the need for credentials entirely. Both Azure Data Factory and Azure Machine Learning support system-assigned managed identities. Granting each identity the Storage Blob Data Contributor role on the ADLS Gen2 account allows read/write access using Azure AD token authentication. No keys, no SAS tokens, no certificates — no credential rotation needed. The identities are tied to the service lifecycle. This is the recommended pattern for service-to-service authentication in Azure.

questions.question: A company is planning to move workloads to Azure but must maintain compliance with data residency requirements — all data must remain within the European Union (EU). How should the architect enforce this at scale across 20 subscriptions?
options: Use Azure Cost Management budget alerts to notify the cloud team whenever resources are deployed outside the approved EU regions
Assign an Azure Policy initiative at the root MG with 'Allowed locations' and 'Allowed locations for resource groups' restricted to EU regions
Configure Azure Blueprints to deploy resource group CanNotDelete locks in EU regions only across the 20 subscriptions
Instruct developers to always select EU regions when deploying resources and rely on training plus a quarterly compliance review
questions.explanation: Data residency enforcement requires a preventive technical control, not a process or detective control. Azure Policy 'Allowed locations' with Deny effect at management group scope blocks resource deployment to any non-EU region across ALL 20 subscriptions automatically. The 'Allowed locations for resource groups' companion policy ensures resource groups themselves can only be created in EU regions (resource groups have a location metadata that determines where group-level metadata is stored). Policy at MG scope covers current and future subscriptions, satisfying the at-scale requirement.

questions.question: An architect must design a solution for an application that requires 500 GB of NVMe SSD storage with consistent sub-millisecond I/O latency for a high-performance SQL workload. The storage must be available only to the specific VM running the SQL workload. Which Azure storage type is appropriate?
options: Azure Managed Disk Premium SSD (P50-P80) — well-proven NVMe-backed performance with consistent P99 latency for SQL workloads
Azure Premium SSD v2 — higher IOPS than Premium SSD with independent configuration of size, IOPS, and throughput per disk
Azure Ultra Disk — sub-millisecond P99 latency with up to 160,000 IOPS configurable independently of disk size, attached to one VM
Azure Files Premium tier exposing SMB shares for the SQL Server data files with cross-VM mount support enabled
questions.explanation: Azure Ultra Disk provides the highest performance tier for Azure managed disks: sub-millisecond I/O latency consistently at P99, up to 160,000 IOPS and 4,000 MB/s throughput per disk, and configurable IOPS/throughput independently of disk size (you can have a 500 GB disk with maximum IOPS). Ultra Disk is exclusively attached to one VM (no shared disk by default). It requires availability zone support and supported VM sizes. Premium SSD v2 also provides high configurable performance but Ultra Disk delivers the lowest guaranteed latency for demanding SQL workloads. Azure Files SMB adds network latency, unsuitable for SQL data files.

questions.question: You must design storage for a workload writing 5 GB log files every minute. The data is read once for analytics within 24 hours, then never touched again but must be retained for 7 years for compliance. Which TWO design choices fit BEST?
options: Write logs to the Hot access tier in ADLS Gen2
Apply a lifecycle policy that moves blobs to Archive after 1 day
Use Premium block blob storage for the entire 7-year retention
Write logs directly to Archive tier and rehydrate them for analytics
questions.explanation: Hot tier is appropriate for the freshly-written data being read within 24h. A lifecycle policy that transitions to Archive after 1 day matches the access pattern (cold for 7 years). Premium is overkill and expensive for cold logs. Writing to Archive directly is impossible — Archive is offline; reading requires rehydration which takes hours.
